extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of natural philosophy, physiology, psychology, and sociology
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the 'law of least resistance' and its application across organic growth, physiology, nervous action, individual choice, economics, and social movements. The text argues that motion and change occur along the resultant of tractive and resistant forces and illustrates this with botanical, physiological, psychological, economic, and sociological examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion follows the line of least resistance / resultant of forces
rubrics_metrics.description: The law that motion follows the line of greatest traction, or the line of least resistance, or the resultant of the two — i.e. when multiple tractive and resistant forces act, the motion takes place in the direction of their resultant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justified by the composition of forces (parallelogram of forces): pairwise resultants reduce many forces to one resultant whose unneutralized component produces motion. Examples and clarifications: if two opposing tractions are unequal the motion is in the direction of the greater; two equal and opposite cause no motion. The persistence of force (force cannot disappear) underlies the deduction. Simple illustrations include two weights over a pulley or two men pulling against each other: the heavier/stronger produces motion in its own direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Root formation by insinuation along interstices (growth via least resistance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Roots grow by insinuating themselves, cell by cell, through the interstices of the soil; they increase by minute additions and wind/twist according to the obstacles they meet, growing most where nutritive materials are added most abundantly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed root appearance (seemingly forced, but actually gradual insinuation); rootlets may exploit interstices created by enlargement of existing roots. Used as an illustration that organic growth follows paths offering least resistance rather than brute force penetration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiral form in organic bodies results from motion under resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: The prevailing spiral form of organic bodies (e.g., rising bubbles, falling bodies in fluids, corkscrew-like paths) indicates that motion under resistance tends to take a spiral direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a rapidly rising bubble in water describes a spiral; branches of many trees show spiral form; leaves around stems are universally spiral in arrangement. The spiral tendency is presented as prima facie evidence for interpreting organic forms by the law of least resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiral arrangement and folding in organs and buds
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific organic structures (young fern leaf curling, imbrication of petals, the heart's spiral commencement) are explained as growth phenomena where curvature, rolling, folding, or spiral turns result from extension under limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and observations: curling up of young fern leaves arises from differential growth; petals imbricate as they grow within a capsule; the heart commences as a spiral turn that can be traced through its chambers—these are interpreted as necessary results of lengthening cellular masses under constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shapes of plants and animals are modified by gravitation (tractive forces must be included)
rubrics_metrics.description: In organic growth, tractive forces such as gravity considerably modify form; branch directions, leaf and flower development, and flexible organ orientations are affected, so the formula for motion/shape is scarcely complete without them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the direction of each branch is altered by Earth's tractive force; flexible organs show directions determined largely by gravity. The text cautions that explanations should include both resisting and tractive forces for completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological channels and flows follow paths of least resistance and are influenced by gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Vessels along which blood, lymph, bile, and secretions flow are channels of least resistance; the currents along them are affected by gravity, producing observable physiological effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: varicose veins, relief of inflamed parts by elevation, congestion of head and face produced by stooping; diurnal variation in peripheral dropsy vs. periorbital oedema show how position alters effects of gravity on transudation through capillaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated neural discharge reduces resistance and forms permanent channels (habits & reflexes)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sensation in one place is habitually followed by a contraction in another, repeated motions diminish resistance along the intervening tissues; each repetition makes the channel easier for subsequent discharge, eventually forming a permanent line of communication (reflex or habit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: discharges produce reactions on traversed tissues that reduce their obstructive power; repetition further diminishes resistance. Consequence: associated ideas and associated actions in the environment become linked in proportion to frequency of co-occurrence—this explains reflex action, habit-formation, and associative learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of muscular excitation in emotion corresponds to least-resistance pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional discharges affect muscles in an order explainable by least-resistance: slight feelings primarily increase cardiac pulsations; stronger feelings affect facial muscles (around the mouth) next; further increase engages respiratory and vocal muscles; strongest passions involve trunk and limb muscles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: laughter is an undirected discharge affecting mouth muscles, then vocal/respiratory muscles, then limbs, then spine—showing that when no special neural route is open, force takes channels of least resistance and, if excessive, proceeds to channels of successively greater resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volition becomes action by completing discharges along pre-established low-resistance neural lines
rubrics_metrics.description: A volition is the representation of movements and sequences which partially arouses sensations and motor nerves; volition is thus an incipient discharge along neural pathways that prior experience has rendered low-resistance, and the passage from volition to action completes that discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: prior experiences and associations make certain transitions from desire to muscle action relatively easy; volitional selection is constrained by which neural channels have been rendered lines of least resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual choice and behaviour aim to minimize total exertion, subject to knowledge and skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The particular muscular movements or courses pursued to reach an object of desire are those implying the smallest total of forces to be overcome; where ignorance or lack of skill leads to more laborious choices, the chosen course is still the one presenting the fewest difficulties relative to the agent's mental state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical corollary: what seems 'least resistance' is relative to an individual's experience and learned channels—experience (personal or communicated) establishes channels of nervous communication that determine perceived options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection implies structural changes along lines of least resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: From a dynamic viewpoint, natural selection causes structural changes in organisms that follow lines of least resistance: multiplication and preservation of kinds or varieties occur where antagonistic forces are least and obstacles are most eluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: populations spread into localities favourable to them where antagonistic forces are fewer; varieties that cope better with surrounding conditions are preserved by continuing movement in directions with fewer obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social growth, migration, and conquest follow directions of least resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: When a society is viewed as an organism, its growth direction is that in which the average of opposing forces is least; tribes and nations spread into tracts with the readiest escape from antagonistic forces, emigrate towards countries with fewest obstacles, and conquer where neighbouring resistance is less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: early large societies in fertile tropical regions; settlement of sea‑shores; emigration to countries with fewer obstacles; migrations of conquered peoples into deserts or mountains only under excess pressure elsewhere. Internal movements (e.g., specialization, trade routes) similarly follow minimization of resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour, exchange, and localization of industry arise from minimizing exertion/cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Barter and specialization begin and spread when they reduce the exertion needed to obtain desired objects; individuals and localities adopt industries that yield the greatest sustenance per unit effort, leading to the localization of industries where production costs are lowest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: choosing to farm/weed/produce those commodities obtainable with the least effort in given local conditions; specialization leads to trade when production plus transit labour is less than local production labour; influx of labour and population growth follow places offering higher returns (less resistance) for given effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport paths and infrastructure follow routes minimizing total obstructive forces (cost/time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paths initially chosen combine shortness with levelness and freedom from obstacles—the smallest total of obstructive forces determines route; subsequent improvements (macadamized roads, canals, railways) further reduce friction and gravity costs; where time matters, a more expensive route may be chosen because time loss equals loss of force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: route choice balances labour of conveyance plus production versus local cost; detours avoid vertical deviations or landowner opposition; after improvements, the chosen road is that with least transit cost (cost as resistance), and where time is critical, trade-offs favor faster (possibly costlier) routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and commercial currents (capital, trade, manufacture) move towards directions of least opposing forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Flows such as capital into high-return businesses, buying cheaply and selling dearly, and adoption of more economical manufacturing modes exemplify movements occurring where opposing forces (cost, friction, inefficiency) are smallest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical restatement: interpret interest or surplus as surplus of products after maintenance of labourers; large surplus implies labour expended with greatest result (i.e. motion evading obstacles). Thus commercial phenomena are complex motions set up along lines of least resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social movements tend to continue once established; complexity increases indirectness
rubrics_metrics.description: Once set up in given directions, social movements tend to continue and persist long after original causes cease; the more complex the social forces involved, the more tortuous and indirect the movements become.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: panics, customs, political agitations, commodities currents persist and require antagonistic forces to arrest them; complexity illustrated by how an artisan's indirect actions can ultimately place a successful businessman into parliament.
